title: Intuitionistic Type Theory
byline: Per Martin-Löf · Padua lectures (1980), Bibliopolis 1984, retypeset edition
note: A short set of lecture notes, one continuous text with numbered topics rather than chapters. Here it is split into its two halves: what the judgements mean, then the rules for each way of forming sets. Summaries are in our own words; the text stays in the PDF.
summary: Martin-Löf lays out a constructive foundation in which propositions are sets, proofs are their elements and elements are programs. The first half explains what it means to judge that something is a set, an element, or equal, starting from canonical elements and the methods that compute them, then extends this to hypothetical judgements and contexts. The second half gives each type former by the same four rules (formation, introduction, elimination, equality): dependent products, dependent sums, finite sets, disjoint union, identity types, natural numbers, lists, well-founded trees and universes. Along the way logic falls out of the types: the axiom of choice becomes provable, and consistency follows from the meaning explanations.

chapters.title: Meaning explanations

sections.title: Introductory remarks
sections.summary: Logic can be symbolism, foundations, or a branch of mathematics; type theory is offered as foundations and doubles as a programming language.

sections.title: Propositions and judgements
sections.summary: A proposition is something that can be proved; a judgement is the act of asserting something about it. The distinction is central.

sections.title: Explanations of the forms of judgement
sections.summary: Each judgement form reads four ways: set and element, proposition and proof, intention and fulfillment, problem and solution.

sections.title: Propositions
sections.summary: A set is given by how its canonical elements are formed and when they are equal; an element is a program that computes a canonical element.

sections.title: Rules of equality
sections.summary: Reflexivity, symmetry, transitivity and the set-equality rules, justified directly from the meanings.

sections.title: Hypothetical judgements and substitution rules
sections.summary: Judgements under one assumption, and the substitution rules that let you plug in elements.

sections.title: Judgements with more than one assumption and contexts
sections.summary: Several assumptions form a context, each depending on the earlier ones.

sections.title: Sets and categories
sections.summary: Families of sets, and the distinction between sets and the larger categories of types.

sections.title: General remarks on the rules
sections.summary: Every type former is given by four kinds of rule, and each rule is justified by the meaning explanations.

chapters.summary: The meaning of the four forms of judgement, from propositions and canonical elements to hypothetical judgements, contexts and the pattern every rule follows.

chapters.title: The set formers

sections.title: Cartesian product of a family of sets
sections.summary: The dependent function type Π: λ-abstraction introduces it, application eliminates it, β-equality connects them.

sections.title: Definitional equality
sections.summary: Definitional equality is the equality of names that the system computes with, as opposed to proved equality.

sections.title: Applications of the cartesian product
sections.summary: Π gives universal quantification, implication and ordinary function spaces; worked derivations of combinators.

sections.title: Disjoint union of a family of sets
sections.summary: The dependent pair type Σ, with pairing and a split eliminator.

sections.title: Applications of the disjoint union
sections.summary: Σ gives existential quantification, conjunction and Cartesian products; real numbers as sequences paired with proofs.

sections.title: The axiom of choice
sections.summary: Under this reading of the quantifiers, the axiom of choice is a theorem with a short constructive proof.

sections.title: The notion of such that
sections.summary: Subsets defined by “such that” are pairs of an element and a proof of the property.

sections.title: Disjoint union of two sets
sections.summary: Binary sum A + B with injections and case analysis; it gives disjunction.

sections.title: Propositional equality
sections.summary: The identity type I(A, a, b) internalizes equality as a set; equality of functions and its limits.

sections.title: Finite sets
sections.summary: Finite sets N₀, N₁, N₂ … given outright; N₀ is falsity, N₂ the Booleans with if–then–else.

sections.title: Consistency
sections.summary: Consistency (⊥ is never true) follows from the meaning explanations, though any metamathematical proof leans on a weaker theory.

sections.title: Natural numbers
sections.summary: Natural numbers with primitive recursion, which also gives proof by induction.

sections.title: Lists
sections.summary: Lists with a recursion operator, defined the same way.

sections.title: Wellorderings
sections.summary: W-types: well-founded trees that give constructive ordinals and transfinite induction.

sections.title: Universes
sections.summary: Universes: a set of (codes for) sets, closed under the type formers, so sets can be quantified over.

chapters.summary: The type formers, each given by formation, introduction, elimination and equality rules, with the logic and mathematics they encode.
